text: {"decision":"GO","artifact":{"author":"Graham Hill","audience":"Business and IT leaders","perspective":"Technical owner only","title":"Valid access does not establish legitimate action","reported_facts":[{"text":"CERT-In reports that attackers used valid credentials from victims’ own whitelisted infrastructure to invoke fund-transfer APIs directly, bypassing application-level checks. Reported transactions included dummy references with no corresponding records.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046"]},{"text":"The subsequent CERT-In advisory reports abuse of legitimate cloud management channels, movement from non-production to production through shared credentials or network paths, and requests originating from shared third-party fetcher IP pools that defeated IP allow-listing.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0058"]},{"text":"In a separate incident, Cloudflare reports that one service token and three accounts stolen during the October 2023 Okta compromise were left unrotated after being mistakenly considered unused. Attackers later used them to access its Atlassian environment. Cloudflare reports that segmentation and other controls limited lateral movement, with no customer data or global network changes affected.","sources":["CF2024"]}],"inference":{"text":"Previously trusted access stops being reliable evidence of legitimate action when an attacker can inherit its credentials, originate requests through its trusted infrastructure, or bypass the checks that connect access to an approved action. A successful authentication or familiar network origin then establishes too little: the technical owner needs evidence that this particular action is authorized and that its required validations occurred.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046","CIAD-2026-0058","CF2024"]},"decision_owned":{"status":"Assumption: hypothetical organizational responsibility","text":"The technical owner decides whether the technical evidence is sufficient to permit a transaction path to operate, or whether it requires containment and revalidation. This responsibility includes verifying credential integrity, isolation between environments, and enforcement of transaction approvals at the API boundary."},"evidence_the_owner_can_see":{"status":"Assumption: availability depends on the organization’s instrumentation and access","items":["Credential inventories, rotation records and authentication logs.","Cloud audit events, deployment changes and evidence of cross-environment access.","API requests linked to approved transaction records, beneficiaries and completed validation stages.","Bank or aggregator reconciliation results and forensic evidence of persistence or log tampering."],"basis":"These evidence categories follow from the attack patterns and recommended controls described by CERT-In; their availability in any particular organization is not established.","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046","CIAD-2026-0058"]},"what_the_technical_owner_must_learn_from_the_business_owner":{"status":"Assumption: hypothetical division of responsibilities","text":"Which records establish a legitimate payment; who may approve beneficiaries, amounts and exceptions; what transaction limits apply; and what interruption or manual-review capacity the business can tolerate. Technical verification depends on those business definitions of authorization."},"hypothetical_illustration":{"status":"Hypothetical illustration, not a reported event","text":"A payout request arrives with a valid token from an approved server, but its reference has no matching sanctioned record. The technical owner should treat the token and server as insufficient evidence of authorization and apply the agreed rejection or hold rule. The business owner supplies the definition of an approved record and the permitted exception process."},"editorial_conclusion":"Require evidence linking each sensitive action to current authorization and completed validation. Treat credentials and network location as inputs to that judgment, rather than sufficient proof."},"claim_support":[{"claim":"Valid credentials and whitelisted infrastructure can coexist with unauthorized transfers.","type":"Reported fact","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046"]},{"claim":"Trusted management channels, shared environment credentials and shared fetcher pools can be abused.","type":"Reported fact","sources":["CIAD-2026-0058"]},{"claim":"Unrotated stolen credentials enabled access in Cloudflare’s separate incident; Cloudflare reports bounded impact.","type":"Reported fact attributed to the victim","sources":["CF2024"]},{"claim":"Access evidence must be connected to action-specific authorization.","type":"Editorial inference","sources":["CIAD-2026-0046","CIAD-2026-0058","CF2024"]},{"claim":"The proposed technical ownership, evidence access and business handoff apply to an illustrative organization.","type":"Explicit assumption","sources":[]}],"limitations":["Based solely on supplied source text; no independent retrieval or verification was performed.","The two CERT-In advisories belong to the same reporting chain; the November advisory updates the October advisory and is not independent corroboration.","Cloudflare provides an independent first-party retrospective account from a different organization, period and system. The comparison supports a bounded conceptual contrast, not a common attacker or universal control-effectiveness claim.","CERT-In recommendations do not demonstrate measured effectiveness. No claim about AI’s causal contribution is needed for this argument.","Only the technical owner perspective is developed, following the explicit perspective restriction. Responsibilities and local evidence availability are assumptions."]}
